body.p: In the Final Office Action mailed on November 29, 2023, claims 1-13 are pending in the application; Claims 1-7 and 11-12 are withdrawn; Claims 8-10 and 13 stand rejected. Claims 8 and 13 are amended. Claims 14-16 are new.
As set forth herein, reconsideration and withdrawal of the rejections and objections of the claims is respectfully requested.

A telephonic interview was conducted with the Examiner on February 28, 2024. Proposed claim amendments to claims 8 and 13 were presented to the Examiner as made of record in the Examiner's Interview Summary dated March 5, 2024. During the interview, the Murphy reference was discussed and it was the Applicant's position that Murphy did not disclose anything that could be reasonably interpreted as the claimed numerical lung scores or scaled lung scores. The Applicant explained that the claim term "score" should be given its normal dictionary definition and an example definition was presented - the Miriam Webster's applicable definition as recited as definition 7a: a number that expresses accomplishment (as in a game or test) or excellence (as in quality) either absolutely in points gained or by comparison to a standard. No agreement was reached as to allowable subject matter with respect to the proposed amended claims 8 and 13.

Claims 8-10 and 13 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over US Patent Publication No. 2006/0201432 (hereinafter referred as Pratt) in view of US Patent Publication No. 2007/0106179 (hereinafter referred as Bagha) further in view of US Patent Publication No. 2004/0236241) (hereinafter referred as Murphy). The Applicant respectfully traverses this rejection.
The Examiner provides the following explanation as to what Murphy teaches with respect to the claimed lung scores (See Office Action, last paragraph page 2 continuing on to page 3);
However, in the rejection, the slope (Fig. 9B, a derived parameter of the data of Fig. 9A) is a lung score, it is scaled by a slope threshold constant which yields a scaled lung score.
This is compared to thresholds (Para [0081] signal slope threshold), which is defined as
corresponding to respiratory conditions (adventitious sounds Para [0081]) indicating the health status of the animal's respiratory condition (Para [0077] the adventitious sounds are
any of crackles, wheeze, or rhonchi, see Table 1)

Claims 8 and 13 are amended to recite additional limitations to include reciting that the lung scores are displayed as whole numbers on the user interface. As explained on pages 11 and 23 of the specification, a spectrogram of the recorded sound data along with a lung score is shown on a user interface. Referring to Fig. 7, a calculated lung score 104 is displayed as a single whole number and in Fig. 8, a scaled lung score 105 is also displayed as a single whole number.

Fig. 9B in Murphy shows a data plot 920 for a particular micro-phone 102 (FIG. 1) plotted as a function of time. The data plot 920 includes a slope data signal 922 and a corresponding slope threshold trace 924. The slope data signal 922 exceeds the slope threshold trace 924 at various points (e.g., points D, E, F, etc.). Within the data plot of Fig. 9B, the slope is shown on the vertical axis and time is plotted on the horizontal axis. With regard to the data points on the data plot, there are a large number of data points and nothing in Murphy correlates any particular data point with a single numerical score or value that could be interpreted to be the score that corresponds to a respiratory condition.

As set forth in the description, e.g., at pages 9 and 10, the preferred embodiment presented there provides scaled lung scores in the form of whole numbers ranging from 1 to 9. These scaled lung scores provide a caregiver with a simple yet reliable indication of the health status of the animal.

As previously argued, paragraph [0081] in Murphy does not describe anything relating to the characterization of lung sounds to determine a health status but rather, this paragraph simply explains how discrete sound artifacts (i.e. noise) is distinguished from "adventitious" sounds (i.e. the targeted sounds from the respiration of the animal). An example slope threshold constant is identified in Murphy (.015) in which the median of the preliminary threshold trace is multiplied by this constant. The resulting value is then added to the preliminary threshold trace to form a slope threshold trace. Next, following the process described with respect to Figs. 8 and 9A and 9B (see [0082-0090]), it is clear that the identification of noise is necessary to obtain measurable sound data from the animal's respiration as opposed to a mixed signal that includes both noise and respiration sounds. The scaling factor mentioned in Murphy at [0081] is not a health status indicator. The scaling factor is applied to the data in order to identify the portions that correspond

to a respiratory condition (adventitious sound detection), but the scaling factor alone does not provide the respiratory condition. The scaling factor is not explained but is assumed to be some mathematical coefficient or value that is combined with the data. Without the data, the scaling factor would presumably be meaningless.

Also with respect to paragraph [0117] in Murphy, a diagnosis is obtained by use of a sound detection program that may be based on a neural network module such as a programming tool from a statistical classification source. The program interacts with a training database to derive the proposed diagnosis. The training database includes data corresponding to the ratio of inspiration to expiration, the numbers and locations of course, medium and fine crackles and wheezes etc. Alternatively, Murphy recites that the program may utilize a multiple logistic regression model to arrive at a proposed diagnosis. Murphy uses a statistical classification method or a logistic regression model but does not disclose any algorithm that utilizes selected frequencies as claimed.
Considering the foregoing, this rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) should be reconsidered and withdrawn.

New claims 14 and 15 depend from claims 8 and 13, respectively, and further recite that the selected frequencies are between about 500-900 Hz. It is respectfully submitted that the cited prior art does not evaluate such selected frequencies in the recited range. Claims 14 and 15 nonetheless should also be considered allowable at least based on their respective dependencies.

New independent claim 16 is introduced which recites a filter protocol in which at least one of three filters are used to filter undesirable noise. It is submitted that the prior art of record does not teach the claimed filter protocol. Even if filtering is concluded by the Examiner to be inherently disclosed in the cited prior art, the prior art of record at least fails to teach the recited ranges of the filtered frequencies with respect to the sounds generated by the sources of noise. Therefore, claim 16 should also be considered allowable.
Based on the foregoing, Applicant believes all pending claims are in condition for allowance and such disposition is respectfully requested.
RESPECTFULLY SUBMITTED, BERG HILL GREENLEAF RUSCITTI LLP
